title: The pledge of Ridwan
hook: Uthman goes into Mecca as envoy and won't circle the Ka'bah without the Prophet; a rumor says he's been killed, and they pledge under a tree, Salamah three times (48:18; Bukhari; Muslim)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the pilgrims turned back: a kneeling camel, a dry well, and a closed door at Hudaybiyyah. Your line was: stopped at the edge. When a door closed, did you take a breath before you pushed? Day seven hundred eighty-five.

Someone has to go into Mecca and talk. In Sahih al-Bukhari, Ibn Umar says the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ sent Uthman ibn Affan, because no one was held in higher regard in Mecca than he was. So Uthman goes in alone, to explain that they've come as pilgrims, not to fight. Then he doesn't come back. Time passes, and a rumor runs through the camp at Hudaybiyyah: Uthman has been killed. Everything depends on what they do next. Today: the pledge of Ridwan.
screen: `UTHMAN GOES IN ALONE.` → `HE DOESN'T COME BACK.` → `A RUMOR: UTHMAN IS DEAD.`

segments.voice: First, a small detail about Uthman, from the early biographers. While he was in Mecca, the Meccans told him: you're here, so go around the Ka'bah if you want to. And he refused. He said he would not circle it until the Messenger of Allah did. The thing they had all walked so far for was in front of him, and he wouldn't take it alone. Meanwhile, back at the camp, the Prophet called the people to pledge. He sat beneath a tree, and they came, one by one, and put their hand in his. Salamah ibn al-Akwa, in Sahih Muslim, tells his own part. He pledged early, among the first. Later, in the middle of the crowd, the Prophet said: pledge, Salamah. I already did, he said. And again, said the Prophet. So he pledged a second time. Near the end, it happened once more. Salamah, won't you pledge? I pledged at the start and in the middle. And again. So he pledged a third time. The sources word the promise differently: Salamah says they pledged unto death; Jabir, also in Muslim, says they pledged not to flee. And for Uthman, who wasn't there, the Prophet held up his right hand and said this is Uthman's hand, and pledged for him. Surah al-Fath gives the moment two verses. One says that those who pledge to the Prophet pledge to Allah, and then, in Pickthall's words: "The Hand of Allah is above their hands." The other says Allah was well pleased with the believers when they pledged beneath the tree. From that verse the pledge takes its name: ridwan, good pleasure. Uthman turned out to be alive. But the pledge had already been made, and made again.
screen: `UTHMAN WON'T CIRCLE THE KA'BAH ALONE.` · `HANDS IN HIS HAND, UNDER A TREE.` · `AND AGAIN, SALAMAH.` · `THE HAND OF ALLAH IS ABOVE THEIR HANDS.` · then, large: `UNDER THE TREE.`

segments.voice: The practice: renew a pledge. Sit, and breathe. Bring to mind a promise you made once and haven't said out loud in a long time: to a spouse, a friend, a child, to your own health, to your faith if you have one. You made it at the start. Now, somewhere in the middle, make it again, quietly, in your own words, the way Salamah did when he was told: and again. If you pray, you can renew it before Allah. If you don't, simply hold the promise in mind. Picture a tree and a hand. The bell holds the time.
Ridwan, good pleasure: the name of the pledge made beneath a tree at Hudaybiyyah, from surah 48:18, Allah was pleased with them. Today's word.
Your line: under the tree. Today, say one old promise again to the person you made it to, even if they never asked. Day seven hundred eighty-five.

howItsDone: Muslims honor the companions of the tree named in 48:18, and the pledge of Ridwan is taught as part of the story of Hudaybiyyah in sirah classes and in commentaries on Surah al-Fath.

original.note: Arabic: good pleasure, approval; the pledge is named after Allah being pleased with the believers in 48:18.

trapdoor: what you thought: an oath before a fight.
what it means: a pledge made under a tree, for a friend feared dead, and made again.
what a scholar hears: 48:10's hand above their hands, 48:18's good pleasure, Salamah's three pledges in Muslim, and the differing wording of the promise.

notes: Pickthall 48:10 phrase quoted from memory; confirm exact wording ('The Hand of Allah is above their hands.').
Uthman's refusal to circle the Ka'bah is from the sirah (Ibn Ishaq), not the major collections; framed as 'from the early biographers'.
'No one was held in higher regard in Mecca than he was' paraphrases Ibn Umar in Bukhari 3698 (if there had been anyone more honored in Mecca than Uthman, he would have sent him); confirm.
Muslim 1807 retold from memory (the three pledges); it also includes the shield Salamah gave to his uncle, left out here. Confirm the details and number.
Year 2 day 582 covered 48:18 and 'this is Uthman's hand' and the lost tree; this day centers on Uthman's refusal and Salamah's renewed pledge.
The practice invites renewing a personal promise 'in your own words', not a new prayer.

Editor: 48:18 uses the verb (radiya), not the word ridwan, so 'that word, pleased, is ridwan' became 'from that verse the pledge takes its name: ridwan, good pleasure' (and the word segment says 'named for 48:18'); cut the stock 'and it's lovely'; 'in the middle of your life' (an age assumption) became 'somewhere in the middle'; the rumor of Uthman's death is now attributed in sources to Ibn Ishaq.
